subject: maths
title: Fractions — add, subtract, multiply, divide

slides.heading: Why fractions need different rules for different operations
slides.body: A fraction represents a part of a whole — the denominator tells you how many equal parts exist, the numerator tells you how many you have. Adding fractions requires a common denominator because you can only combine parts of the same size, but multiplying does not — you are scaling one fraction by another.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The four operations at a glance
slides.formula: Add/Subtract: find LCD, convert, then ±numerators | Multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom | Divide: Keep, Change, Flip
slides.formulaExplained: For addition and subtraction, rewrite both fractions with the lowest common denominator (LCD) before combining numerators. For multiplication, multiply numerators together and denominators together — no common denominator needed. For division, keep the first fraction unchanged, change ÷ to ×, then flip (invert) the second fraction.
slides.whenToUse: Use the correct rule for each operation — the most common error is using the addition method when multiplying.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Work out 2¼ ÷ 1½. Give your answer as a mixed number.

steps.instruction: Convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Apply Keep, Change, Flip: keep 9/4, change ÷ to ×, flip 3/2 to 2/3.
Multiply and simplify: numerators 9×2=18, denominators 4×3=12. Simplify 18/12.
Convert the improper fraction to a mixed number.
steps.working: 3/2: 2 goes into 3 once with remainder 1. So 3/2 = 1½.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Adding numerators and denominators separately when adding fractions — e.g. writing 1/3 + 1/4 = 2/7 instead of finding LCD = 12 to get 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.
mistakes.correction: You can never add denominators. Find the lowest common denominator first, convert both fractions, then add numerators only.

mistakes.mistake: Flipping the first fraction instead of the second when dividing — e.g. for 5/8 ÷ 3/4, writing 8/5 × 3/4 instead of 5/8 × 4/3.
mistakes.correction: Keep, Change, Flip means: keep the FIRST fraction exactly as it is, then flip only the SECOND fraction.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing — e.g. multiplying whole parts and fraction parts separately: 2¼ × 1½ treated as (2×1) + (1/4 × 1/2) = 2 + 1/8 = 2⅛ instead of 9/4 × 3/2 = 27/8 = 3⅜.
mistakes.correction: Always convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first: whole × denominator + numerator, written over the denominator.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: To add or subtract fractions, find the lowest common denominator, convert both fractions, then combine numerators only — never add the denominators.
keyFacts.examTip: If the denominators share no obvious factor, multiply them together to get a valid (if not lowest) common denominator.

keyFacts.fact: To multiply fractions, multiply top × top and bottom × bottom. Common denominators are not needed.
keyFacts.examTip: Simplify by cancelling diagonally before multiplying — it keeps numbers smaller and reduces errors.

keyFacts.fact: To divide fractions: Keep the first fraction, Change ÷ to ×, Flip the second fraction. Then multiply as normal.
keyFacts.examTip: KCF (Keep-Change-Flip) — the most likely place to lose a mark is flipping the wrong fraction.

keyFacts.fact: To convert a mixed number to an improper fraction: (whole number × denominator) + numerator, written over the original denominator. E.g. 3¼ = 13/4.
keyFacts.examTip: Always convert to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing mixed numbers — operating on the whole and fraction parts separately gives the wrong answer.
